The effect of folic acid and pteridine analogs on rates of [3H]cAMP secretion, monitored by rapid perfusion, was studied. At low cell densities folic acid elicited only minimal [aH]cAMP secretion. At high cell densities, folic acid elicited greater increases in cellular CAMP and rates of [3H]cAMP secretion than did maximally effective doses of CAMP. Starvation triggers a developmental program; initially the amoebae become specialized to communi- cate via extracellular 3’,5’-cyclic adenosine monophos- phate (CAMP). Chemotaxis toward the nucleotide me- diates the aggregation of up to lo6 cells to form mul- ticellular structures. Time-lapse observation of this highly coordinated process suggests that the chemo- tactic signals are relayed through the monolayer for long distances (up to 3 cm).

Furthermore, waves of CAMP, which emanate from cen- ters with a regular periodicity of 5 to 10 min have been visualized in monolayers of aggregating amoebae (Tom- chik and Devreotes, ; reviewed in Devreotes, ).

Early in development, cell mono- layers divide into territories of -lo6 cells and cells within the territory aggregate to the center. Aggre- gation is mediated by extracellular adenosine 3’:5’- cyclic monophosphate (CAMP).

Periodically secreted by cells in the center of a territory, CAMP diffuses to nearby cells and binds to high-affinity surface receptors, leading to transient activation of adenylate cyclase. The result is a rise in intracellular CAMP which is rapidly secreted. Referred to as the CAMP signaling response, this process is repeated in more distal cells and produces a coordinated cell-to-cell relay of CAMP in the form of CAMP waves which propagate through the monolayer.

Introduction How cells sense and move along chemical gradients, referred to as directed migration or chemotaxis, is one of the fundamental questions in cell biology. This fascinating process plays a crucial role in normal physiological as well as pathological events, from the proper functioning of the immune system to cancer metastasis [1].

A consensus has emerged that in order to understand chemotaxis, we must be able to answer several separable but interrelated questions [4]. What drives spontaneous cell motility? How do cells read external chemoattractant gradients?

In biology, the classical model of an excitable system is that proposed by Hodgkin and Huxley to explain the ‘all-or-nothing’ characteristic of action potentials in neurons [6]. Perturbations of excitable systems can be either subthreshold, simply dying out, or superthreshold, eliciting a full response. When the excitable elements are spatially distributed, as they are along an axon, the system is said to be an excitable medium.
